analysis.one_liner: Bans Members of Congress and their families from owning or trading individual stocks and similar investments.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in March 2025 with 5 cosponsors, was sent to four House committees and has received no hearing, markup, or vote; Congress remains in session through January 2027.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal for a Member of Congress, their spouse, or their dependent children to own or trade individual stocks, bonds, commodities, futures, options, or hedge fund interests. Current members would have 180 days after the law takes effect to sell off banned assets (90 days for new members, and up to 5 years for hedge fund and private fund stakes). Members would keep broad exceptions: they could still hold widely held diversified index funds, Treasury bonds, retirement accounts, small business stakes, and assets tied to a spouse's own job. Violations could draw civil penalties of up to $100,000 per offense, enforced by the Attorney General or the Special Counsel. The bill has only been introduced and referred to committees; no committee has acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: The general public and the integrity of financial markets. Lawmakers constantly handle information that moves stock prices — upcoming regulations, tariffs, subsidies, and contract decisions — and the bill would remove the personal incentive to trade on that knowledge by barring members and their immediate families from holding or trading individual securities.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits Members of Congress, their spouses, and dependent children from owning or trading any stock, bond, commodity, future, security, hedge fund interest, derivative, or option, with required divestment of existing holdings [S2]

Sets divestment deadlines — 180 days for sitting members, 90 days for future members, and 180 days for assets received mid-service such as an inheritance, with up to 5 years for hedge fund and venture capital stakes [S2]
Allows enforcement by the Attorney General or the Special Counsel, with a civil penalty of up to $100,000 per violation, on top of any other criminal or civil remedies [S2]

Preserves ordinary retirement-style investing by permitting widely held diversified investment funds that present no conflict of interest, Treasury bills, notes, and bonds, and government retirement plan funds [S2]
Defers capital gains tax on assets sold specifically because the ban required divestment, so members are not taxed twice on a forced sale [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Members of Congress and their immediate families, who would have to sell individual stocks, options, commodity positions, and hedge fund stakes within set deadlines and could face civil fines of up to $100,000 per violation for trading or holding them afterward.
analysis.who_pays_short: Members of Congress and their families

drawbacks.text: The penalty is a fine of at most $100,000 per violation, which may be small relative to the wealth of some members and depends on future administrations choosing to enforce it [S2]
Members may still own interests in hedge funds and venture capital funds — the most opaque vehicles — for up to five years before divesting [S2]
A spouse may keep trading assets used in the course of the spouse's own primary occupation, a carve-out that could shelter meaningful holdings from the ban [S2]
A blanket ownership ban may deter some people with substantial investments or financial careers from serving in Congress at all, an objection supporters of narrower disclosure rules raise [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is straightforward: members would give up the ability to invest in individual companies in exchange for removing a built-in conflict of interest between their legislative work and their family's portfolio. The exceptions are broad enough that members could still build wealth through diversified index funds and Treasuries, so the practical cost is modest. The design has soft spots — a $100,000 fine cap, a five-year runway for hedge fund stakes, and a spouse-occupation exception — but the main risk is not the text of the bill; it is that it has gone nowhere.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to four House committees, then sent to one subcommittee, and none of them has taken it up for a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Burchett (R-TN) introduced the End Congressional Stock Trading Act in the House on March 6, 2025 [S1][S4]
The bill was referred to four committees — Financial Services, and in addition Agriculture, House Administration, and Ways and Means — so any one of them can hold it without action [S4]
On March 28, 2025, it was referred to the Financial Services Subcommittee on Commodity Markets, Digital Assets, and Rural Development; no hearing, markup, or vote has followed [S4]
Five Republicans have cosponsored the bill, and no further cosponsors have been added [S3]
The 119th Congress runs through January 3, 2027, so the bill could still move, but as of the current record it has not advanced past committee referral [S1]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Members of Congress and their families keep the ability to hold and trade individual stocks, options, commodities, and private fund stakes while their legislative work can move those markets. No committee chair has been required to act.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Members of Congress and their families

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors are Republicans, but the bill has drawn no recorded opposition, and no member of either party has been forced to vote on it [S3].

industries.note: The bill's direct targets are the members themselves: they would have to divest individual stocks, options, commodities, and hedge fund interests within set deadlines and face civil fines up to $100,000 per violation. Their institutional interest in keeping that trading ability is the reason the bill needs committee action to move, and it has received none [S2][S4].

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private investment funds
industries.note: Members' families could not hold hedge fund or venture capital interests under the bill, though they get a five-year runway to exit, and spouses may keep trading assets used in their own occupation. The effect on the funds themselves is marginal [S2].

analysis.trajectory: With only five cosponsors, no Democratic support on the record, and four committees holding it without a hearing, the bill is unlikely to advance on its own. Its realistic path is being folded into a broader stock-trading bill that House or Senate leadership decides to schedule; absent that, it will sit in committee until this Congress ends in January 2027.
